### Operationalize the admission test, not another writing ritual

For consolidation, apply the admission test to each candidate correction. For later landings, apply it to each proposed addition or substantive edit. An established trap can reuse its evidence; do not rerun a baseline merely to satisfy a form. When necessity is uncertain, use a fresh-reader test.

A small Claude Workflow could separate three jobs: a scenario author establishes the expected decision and its evidence; fresh readers answer neutral matched scenarios with and without the candidate correction; a grader compares answers against the evidence. For an incremental edit, the baseline should normally be the existing skill **without the candidate**, not an entirely unassisted worker. Otherwise the test cannot show that this particular addition is needed. A no-skill baseline remains useful for discovering broader pretraining assumptions.

The scenario author and grader may see the record; test readers must not see the expected answers or each other's responses. Require correct decisions and scope, not recitation. A candidate earns space when it addresses an evidenced wrong assumption or consequential missing knowledge; if the baseline already handles the case, seek evidence from other relevant failures before retaining it. One passing answer is not proof that every future worker will know it.

This is a workflow outline for Claude to reconcile with the recovered run, not a claim about how that run was implemented. Keep the writer's instruction small: **identify the mistaken assumption, show why it is expected, and verify that the correction prevents the mistake without introducing another.** Preserve evaluation evidence in maintenance records. usage: facts-extract.sh [--check] [--part N] [--page-bytes N] [--root DIR] [--common] [QUERY ...]

Prints what the queries name, whole and in the order they are given; a rung's
briefing is one such command. Each piece comes under a line naming its file
and section. The output comes in parts of at most PAGE_BYTES (default 28000);
part 1 opens with the size of the whole output in bytes and estimated tokens,
then what was asked for, where it is and what was not found; each part says
whether there is a next one, and --part N prints part N.

QUERY is one of:
  F-87, P-48             the entry of that number in FACTS.md or POSITIONS.md
  F-87+                  the entry, then each entry it points to and each entry
                         that points to it, each once, one level
  history:F-87           the entry's blocks in FACTS-history.md or
                         POSITIONS-history.md, oldest first: the provenance line
                         of each change and the line it replaced
  TITLE                  the FACTS.md entry whose title holds TITLE: an entry's
                         title is its bold opening, or where it has none, its
                         opening words up to the first colon, semicolon or full
                         stop; when no current title holds it, the entry one of
                         whose former titles (in FACTS-history.md) does, with a
                         line saying it was retitled
  section:HEADING        every entry of the FACTS.md section whose heading holds HEADING
  index:WORDS            the INDEX.md lines that hold every one of WORDS (at most 10)
  ledger:ROW             row ROW of the gap ledger, whole, under its section and
                         the table's header
  ledger-find:WORDS      one line for each gap ledger row that holds every one of
                         WORDS: its number, its status and the first 150 characters
                         of its claim (at most 10, then how many more matched)
  positions:TITLE        the entry of POSITIONS.md whose bold title holds TITLE, as
                         a TITLE query does in FACTS.md, former titles included;
                         exactly one must, else the nearest titles are named
  positions:DATE WORDS   the entry of POSITIONS.md dated DATE (YYYY-MM-DD, the first
                         date in the entry) whose head, the entry's text up to its
                         first colon and space, holds every one of WORDS; when no
                         entry of POSITIONS.md matches, the entry of
                         POSITIONS-history.md, from the latest of its sections
                         that hold one, with the line saying what became of
                         it; the output says which file it came from
  map:FILE#HEADING       the section of explorations/coordinator/map/FILE whose
                         heading holds HEADING, down to the next heading of its level
  doc:PATH#HEADING       the same for any note, PATH from the repository root, such
                         as a judge's ruling; doc:PATH alone prints the whole note;
                         in a .tex or .tick file the headings are its \chapter, \section,
                         \subsection, \subsubsection and \paragraph titles,
                         matched with their macros dropped; a heading equal to
                         HEADING wins over the headings that merely hold it, and
                         HEADING may be a path, A > B, for B's section inside A's
  map:FILE#HEADING@WORDS, doc:PATH#HEADING@WORDS
                         only the table rows and list items of that section that
                         hold every one of WORDS, a row under its table's header,
                         and the paragraphs whose bold lead holds them
  code:PATH#FROM         the declaration that starts on the one line of PATH that
                         holds FROM, with its line numbers: in .java, .scala and
                         .js through the brace that closes it, elsewhere (.fss,
                         .fsi) through its more indented lines and its end
  code:PATH#FROM..TO     from the declaration at FROM through the end of the
                         one at the first line after it that holds TO
WORDS match as whole words, or as the start of one when a word ends in *.

# The library

The library is `Library/` and `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`, without the compiler's own files there:

- In `Library/`: the interpreter's prelude, `FortressLibrary.fss` and `.fsi`, and its other components. The compiler's `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerAlgebra` and `CompilerSystem` are not part of it. `FortressAst.fss` and `.fsi` are generated from `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast`: edit that file, never these two.
- In `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`: `FortressBuiltin`, `NativeArray` and the rest. The compiler's `CompilerBuiltin` is not part of it.
- `LibraryBuiltin/AnyType`, the top type, belongs to both libraries. After an edit to it, also take the compiled path's step (`build-and-caches.md`, "After an edit of the library").
- `Library/incomplete/` is not on the source path (`default_repository/configuration`), so no program can import what it declares. Nothing that the suites or the model program run imports `Library/GeneratorLibrary.fss` either. Before you cite a declaration as the library's way, check that a running program can reach it.

## How loops and reductions call the library

The desugarer, which both paths share, turns these forms into calls of the library:

- `for x <- g do b end` becomes `g.loop(fn x => b)`, a call of the generator's `loop` method. Each further generator nests one more `loop` call inside.
- `while x <- e do b end` becomes `while __whileCond(e, fn x => b) do end`. `if x <- e then ... end` becomes a call of `__cond`.
- A comprehension or a big operator, such as `SUM`, becomes a call of `__bigOperator`, whose argument calls `__generate` on each generator. So does a big operator inside another: no desugaring calls the library's `__bigOperator2`.

These functions work on the library's generators and reductions: `trait Generator` and `trait Reduction` in `FortressLibrary.fsi`, and `RangeInternals.fss` for ranges. `FortressLibrary.fss` also defines `__loop`, but no desugaring calls it. So a failure inside a loop or a reduction is most often in the library's code, and its fix is a library edit.

## The curator's decisions on the library

- Scalar ranges are over `ZZ32` only. A range over another integer type is a static error, and walk stops when it builds one. Write a wider counter as a `ZZ32` loop that widens its index.
- `ZZ32` and numerals convert into `RR64` implicitly. `ZZ64` converts into `RR64` only explicitly, by `asFloat`.
- For arithmetic that wraps on overflow, use the wrapping operators ∔ `DOTPLUS`, ∸ `DOTMINUS` and ⨰ `DOTTIMES`. Parenthesise every such expression fully, because their precedence is stated only among themselves.
- `SUM` and `PROD` are generic over `AdditiveGroup` and `MultiplicativeRing`. Write the element type wherever generators stand in brackets, also where the generators, the body or a declared type fix it: `SUM[\ZZ32\][j <- 0#n] f(j)`. The checker refuses a call without it (ledger row 731). Walk runs such a call at its value's declared type, or else at the join of its elements' run-time types. An empty `SUM` with no static argument written and no declared type gives the integer 0, and an empty `PROD` the integer 1, whatever the body's type (ledger row 716). With a static argument written that is not a number type, such as a user group, an empty or filtered `SUM` ends in `CastError` (ledger row 436).
- An indexed type's index parameter is bounded by `Index` (`revival-changes.md`, "Traits and objects"). `BoundedRange[\I\]` cannot take the bound, because the open range `(:)` stays a range over `Any` (P-56). So its `atMost(n: I): FullRange[\I\]` has the condition `where { I extends Index }`, which each call must meet (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi`). A type whose static parameter is a range's index type takes the bound too, as `UniformDistribution[\T extends Index\]` over a `FullRange[\T\]` (`Library/Random.fsi`).
- An array's `fill` takes a value, and its `tabulate` a function of the index: `array[\ZZ32\](4).fill(0)`, `array[\ZZ32\](4).tabulate(fn (i:ZZ32):ZZ32 => 10 i)`. The factories that take a function are `tabulatedArray1` to `tabulatedArray3` and `tabulatedVector`.

## Designing a change

- Put each extension into this library, outside the compiler's files. This includes an extension that only the model program needs.
- Fix a gap in the library, not by a workaround in the program that meets it. Take the design from the library's practice as well as from the specification's text. If the two disagree, do as `specification.md`, "When the text and an implementation disagree", says.
- If a rule of the language or the checker refuses the way that you want, find how the library writes that kind of thing. Do the same. The checker's refusals of this library reach you through your brief, or through a run of the count stage (`compiler.md`): `fortress typecheck` checks against the compiler's prelude.
- When you add a method, make it dotted or functional as its family in the library does. If the family shows no practice, follow the team's proposal, which no program can import (`Library/incomplete/Collection.fss`): an updater, a getter or a setter, indexing included, is dotted, and every other method is functional.
- A new functional method reserves its name in every program that imports the library. The phase that binds names then refuses each program that names a variable or a parameter after it: "Variable even is already declared."
- A `fail` without a static argument has the result type `Any`. Where it must have a type, write the static argument, as `strToInt` calls `fail[\ZZ32\]`.
- A dotted method shadows a top-level function of the same name (`overloading.tex`, "Principles of Overloading").
- In an api, declare each top-level function and each member of a trait or object at the header that the component gives it. A function's header is its name, its static parameters with their bounds, its modifiers, its `throws` clause, its parameters' modifiers and types, and its return type. A function's parameters' names and a `where` clause do not count, but each static parameter's name counts (ledger row 836). Give an object's value parameters the api's names, because they are its fields (`compiler.md`, "Traps of the compiled path"). In the cases below, change the component's header to the api's, not the api's to the component's. The examples are in `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi` and `Library/FortressLibrary.fss`.
  - The member's body already answers the api's type. `RR64`'s `opr |\self/|`, `opr |/self\|` and `truncate` answer `ZZ64`, because they call `Float`'s natives, which answer `ZZ64` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fss:184-191`).
  - The api cannot name the component's type. `Array2`'s and `Array3`'s `bounds` and `zeroIndices` answered types of `RangeInternals`, which depends on this api. They now answer the api's `CompactFullRange` types, which those types extend.
  - The api's type is wider, and the overrides and bodies use only that type. `DelegatedIndexed`'s `generator` answers the api's `Generator[\E\]`, as `FlatString`'s override does.

  In the api, write `abstract` on each member that the component leaves without a body.
- The compiled checker's export check matches each api member with a component member of the same name and header. It matches these members in these ways:
  - A field, as `x: ZZ32` in an api's trait: by a component field of its name, its type and its modifiers other than `var`. A component's getter does not match it, so declare a field in the component too (ledger row 842).
  - An object's value parameter: by its type and its modifiers other than `var`, but not by its name.
  - A getter written `abstract`, as `abstract getter one(): T`: by a component getter at its header, or by a component field of its name and type that is neither `hidden` nor `private`. A `hidden` field has no getter.
  - Another member written `abstract`: by a component member at the api's header, with a body or without one.

  Each entry of the check's error names a trait or object and only its first member that differs. After you fix that member, check again to see the next. These steps run the check:
  - For a component of a compiled program or test: `fortress compile`.
  - For the one library's `FortressLibrary` component: the count stage (`compiler.md`, "The checker's time").
  - For the other thirteen components that the gate's distance stage checks: that stage. When a rung needs it, the brief gives its command.
  - For another component of the one library: no step, until the switch-over.
- A new overload can make walk refuse every program at load. `interpreter.md`, "What walk checks", lists what walk refuses.
- Write a new native as a public static method of a class under `nativeHelpers/`, and bind it with `builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.Class.method")`. Both paths run it. Give it the Java types that carry the declared types (`interpreter.md`, "Natives"). Write a glue class under `interpreter/glue/prim/`, which only walk runs, only where no Java type carries a declared type, as for `IntLiteral`'s bindings. A native is an edit of Java: rebuild (`build-and-caches.md`, "Two layers of code"), and test it on both paths (`compiler.md`, "Natives").
- `interpreter.md`, "The model program", says how to check microGPT under walk.

## Editing

A comment after a declaration that ends in an expression or a type becomes part of that declaration's source span. It also becomes part of the unambiguous name made from the span. So a comment-only edit changes the syntax tree. Before you compare parse trees or diagnostics across such an edit, map their positions back to the lines before the edit. Three removed scripts did this: `parse-compare.sh`, `ast-compare.py` and `remap-lines.py`. Print one with `git show ab067d9b6^:explorations/compile-ladder/rung-library-comments/<name>`.

# The compiled checker, the code generator and the runtime

**count stage**
: Script that runs the compiled checker over the interpreter's library, on the `FortressLibrary` component and the apis that it imports, and prints the errors in a table: `explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh`. Its total is the checker count.

**distance stage**
: Stage of the gate that runs the compiled checker over fourteen components of the interpreter's library, `FortressLibrary` among them, runs each of the checker's steps on each component whatever the earlier steps report, and prints the errors in a table. Your brief gives its command when you need it.

The code of this area is in these directories:

- `scala_src/typechecker/`: the type checker, in Scala.
- `compiler/`: the disambiguator, the desugarers, overloading, `codegen/`, `NamingCzar` and `OverloadSet`.
- `runtimeSystem/`: `InstantiatingClassloader`, tasks and transactions.

The phases' names in the code are parse, PREDISAMBIGUATEDESUGAR, DISAMBIGUATE, GRAMMAR, PRETYPECHECKDESUGAR, INTEGERLITERALFOLDING, TYPECHECK, DESUGAR, OVERLOADREWRITE and CODEGEN.

## What the two paths share

After the phases, each path has its own code for these:

- Values: walk's `interpreter/evaluator/values/` (`FInt`, `FFloat`), and the compiled `compiler/runtimeValues/` (`FZZ32`, `FRR64`).
- Number natives: walk's glue classes, in `interpreter/glue/prim/` (`Int.java`, `Long.java`).
- Dispatch: walk searches at run time, in `OverloadedFunction`. The compiled path calls a dispatch method that `OverloadSet` generates.
- The run: `fortress run` starts a second JVM (`bin/run`), which never enters `Shell.java`.

Both paths run the helpers of `nativeHelpers/` (`simpleIntArith.java`) ("Natives").

The phases differ too: walk turns off some desugarings that the compiled path runs (`interpreter.md`, "Where a fix of walk belongs"). A fix of one of those desugarers changes only the compiled path.

## The compiler's prelude, until the switch-over

The compiled path uses the compiler's own prelude: `LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss`, `Library/CompilerLibrary.fss` and `Library/CompilerAlgebra.fss`. `Library/CompilerSystem.fss` is the compiled path's `System`.

Do not add a declaration to the three prelude files: they are deleted at the switch-over. Their tests stay. If a helper of `nativeHelpers/` that the one library binds is wrong, fix the helper's Java, even where the prelude binds it too. Do not edit the prelude's text: its binding then gives the fixed result. If a compiled test pinned the old result, change the test with the helper, as for any fixed defect.

## What the compiled path cannot compile yet

For a construct that it cannot compile yet, the code generator calls `sayWhat` or throws another `CompilerError`. Such a call or throw is a code-generator wall. The code generator has no case for these constructs:

- `label` and `exit`, `spawn`, and `atomic` used as an expression;
- an object expression;
- an array literal, such as `[1 2 3]`.

It compiles a local function as a closure, also one that calls itself or another local function of its block. It refuses these forms (ledger row 304):

- a local function with static parameters of its own: 'Can't compile a local function with static parameters of its own yet';
- two local functions of one name in a block: 'Can't compile overloaded local functions yet';
- a local function with the `atomic` modifier: 'Can't compile a local function with this modifier yet'.

A type assumption `e asif T` has the value of `e`, but the call around it chooses its declaration as if `e` were a `T`, a supertype of `e`'s type (`Specification/basic/expressions/type-annotation.tex`). The code generator compiles one at a dotted call's receiver, at a call of a functional method or an overloaded function whose every argument is an assumption, and elsewhere as the value of `e`. It refuses these forms (ledger row 818):

- a call of a functional method or an overloaded function with an assumption at some of its arguments but not all: 'Can't compile a dispatched call whose arguments are not all type assumptions';
- a generic method on an assumed receiver: 'Can't compile a type assumption at the receiver of a generic method yet';
- a call of an overloaded generic function with an assumption at an argument: 'Can't compile a type assumption at a call of an overloaded generic function yet'.

It also refuses a function or method with a contract (`requires`, `ensures`, `invariant`). It compiles a declaration whose own header or `extends` entry has a `where` clause, and emits nothing for the clause. A call of a function or method whose own clause introduces a `where`-clause variable, as `where [\nat n\]` does, links, but dies at run time with `NoClassDefFoundError` (ledger row 867). `compiler_tests/XXXWhereVariableCallCompiled.test` records it: copy its form for such a call. The disambiguator, which both paths run, drops a trait's or object's contract, so the code generator never sees one, and walk does not check one either (ledger row 781). It refuses a function or method with a modifier other than `getter`, `setter`, `io`, `private`, `abstract` and `test`, such as `override` (ledger row 650). A trait or object that extends a generic trait compiles with `Any` as the static argument. With `Bottom`, `Self` or an abbreviated type there, the code generator refuses the declaration. An abbreviated type is a short form that the specification gives for a type, such as `RR64[3]` for an array type. With a tuple that holds `Any` there, the code generator crashes (ledger row 889).

The compiler's prelude has no array types, only `ZZ32Vector` and `StringVector`. Its `for` loops, comprehensions and reductions work over `ZZ32` ranges only. Its reductions give a `ZZ32` or a `String`.

Until the switch-over, a compiled test uses none of these. If a test needs one, write it as an `XXX` test that names the wall (`tests-writing.md`).

## What the code generator does

`SKILL.md`, "The compiled runtime", gives the jars, the dispatch methods, the templates and the boxed numbers.

- It emits no primitive `double` arithmetic.
- The class loader rewrites a template's bytes with ASM. The emitted classfiles stay at version 1.6, because this rewriting keeps no stack-map frames. Do not raise the version.
- The `value` modifier adds the mark interface `ValueObjectMark` to the object's class. The compiled `SEQV` (`nativeHelpers/equality.java`) reads the mark. The modifier does not inline or unbox the fields.
- An array of `RR64` values is to be stored as an unboxed `double[]`. The code generator does not build it yet (`SKILL.md`, "The compiled runtime"). If your task touches how arrays are stored, print the two POSITIONS entries on arrays first (about 2 KB):

      explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'positions:array is stored as' 'positions:array design'

## The runtime

- The class loader is `runtimeSystem/InstantiatingClassloader.java`. The revival has changed it for sizes and for the lock on a class's first load (ledger row 417). Before you investigate a failure while a class loads, read ledger rows 408 and 559, which name it (`records.md`, "Reading the record").
- The compiled code keeps each mutable variable in a cell (`compiler/runtimeValues/MutableFValue.java`). Before each read and write of the cell, the generated code asks `BaseTask.inATransaction()` (`runtimeSystem/`). Inside an `atomic` block, the access goes through the transaction. So the transaction tracks the variables that the block touches.

## Natives

`import java com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.{...}` in a `.fss` file binds static Java methods over plain Java values.

A body `builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.Class.method")` binds one such method, a helper, too. In a compile, at the parse, the compiled path, and not walk, rewrites the body as a call of the method through a generated `import java`, with `self` first in a trait or object (`compiler/BuiltinPrimitiveRewriter.java`). The checker then checks the declaration against the method's Java signature. In a compile, it reads `int` as `ZZ32`, `long` as `ZZ64`, `float` as `RR32`, `double` as `RR64`, `boolean` as `Boolean`, `String` as `JavaString`, `BigInteger` as `ZZ` and `Object` as `Any` (`NamingCzar.fortressTypeForForeignJavaType`). Which commands rewrite is below the list. Walk calls the same method by reflection (`interpreter.md`, "Natives"). The compile stops in these cases:

- If the string is in that package but names no public static method: 'builtinPrimitive names no static helper: …'.
- If the string names a glue class or anything else outside that package: 'Variable builtinPrimitive is not defined.'
- If the declaration has a varargs parameter: the same message (ledger row 849).
- If the declaration is a local function or a method of an object expression: the same message. The rewrite reaches only a component's declarations and the members of its traits and objects (ledger row 865).

The rewrite runs only in a JVM that has made a Fortress repository of the compiled path, the compiler's store of components, not this git repository. Walk's repository switches it off again. `fortress compile` makes one, and so do `disambiguate`, `grammar`, `desugar` and `typecheck` (`Shell.compilerPhases`). `fortress parse` and `fortress api` make none, so they rewrite a body only after a compile in the same JVM (ledger row 882). Alone, they pass a misspelt helper. Test a binding with `compile`. In a suite, the result of `parse` or `api` depends on whether a compile ran earlier in the same JVM.

To test a helper on the compiled path, write a compiled test whose own declarations bind it, as `compiler_tests/NativeHelperBindingCompiled.fss` does. Until the switch-over, a compiled test cannot reach the interpreter's library's bindings.

The count stage and the distance stage check the interpreter's library with the same rewrite. There, the checker differs from a compile in these ways:

- A string that names a glue class, or a declaration with a varargs parameter, does not stop the check. The body stays a call of `builtinPrimitive`, typed at the declared result type, and no Java signature checks it (ledger row 849).
- The checker reads a helper's Java types as the interpreter's library's types: `String` as `String`, not `JavaString`, and the rest as in a compile.
- A component that imports a DSL grammar is parsed by other code (`GraphRepository.syntaxExpand`), which does not rewrite its bindings. So, as for a glue class, no Java signature checks them.
- The count stage checks only the `FortressLibrary` component's bindings. A binding of another component, as `FortressBuiltin`'s, only the distance stage checks.

The checker, in a compile and in both stages, reads `int` as `NN32` or `Char`, and `long` as `NN64`, only for six transfer helpers with fixed names (`NamingCzar.java:373-384`, `:494-503`). Examples are `makeNN32FromZZ32WithSpecialCompilerHackForNN32ResultType` for a result and `makeZZ32FromNN32WithSpecialCompilerHackForNN32ArgumentType` for a parameter. ## Traps of the compiled path

- The compiler's prelude declares `print`, `println` and `String`'s `||` at `Object`, not `Any` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi:37`, `:55`, `:61`). So until the switch-over, the checker refuses a generic that prints a value of a type parameter written without a bound, or concatenates it onto a `String`. The message names `Object`, as 'Object->() is not applicable to an argument of type T.' does for `println`. In such a generic of a compiled program or test, write `T extends Object`. The generic then takes no tuple, function or `()`. The one library declares these operations at `Any` or `String`, so do not change its text for this limit.
- A `try`'s `forbid` clause lists exception types: an exception of a listed type that no `catch` clause took is wrapped in a `ForbiddenException`, which the `try` throws. A `try`'s `finally` clause does not run when an exception leaves the `try` block: one that no `catch` clause takes, or that `ForbiddenException` (ledger row 890). So write no compiled program that relies on `finally` after an exception leaves the `try`. A test that needs it is an `XXX` test (`tests-writing.md`). In a `try` nested in another `try` of one body, the outer `try`'s `catch` clause is matched first (ledger row 888). A `try` whose block can throw, with a `finally` clause and no `catch` or `forbid` clause, fails with a `VerifyError` at class load (ledger row 891).
- An api and the component that implements it must have the same name. The linker looks for a component with the api's own name. If there is none, the link fails ("Could not find an implementation for API"), and the run dies with `NoClassDefFoundError`.
- The compiled dispatch ignores the contravariance of a parameter of arrow type. The property `fortress.disable.contravariance` is true by default, so `OverloadSet` passes no variance. The team turned it off in 2012 (`c35aac139`). If a compiled call with function arguments picks another declaration than walk does, look here first.
- A clean link does not prove that every call has its method. Two calls die at run time with `NoSuchMethodError`:
  - a call of a functional method of an object that a trait's `comprises` clause lists, on a value whose static type is the object. An example is `num(R)`, where `trait Q comprises { R }` declares `abstract num(self): ZZ32` and `object R extends Q` gives its body. Call it through a value typed as the trait, as `q: Q = R` and then `num(q)` (ledger row 815);
  - a read of an exported object's value parameter, from a component that imports the api, where the exporting component names the parameter otherwise than the api. A value parameter is a parameter of the object's constructor, and also a field. An example is `Np(3).a`, where the api declares `object Np(a: ZZ32)` and the component `object Np(z: ZZ32)`. The export check compares no value parameter's name. Give each value parameter the api's name (ledger row 839).

`revival-changes.md` gives the rules. This section gives where the checker applies them, and where it does not yet.

Inside a static argument, as `T` in `Box[\T\]`, the parameter stays. The paths differ on `tint[\T extends Red\](x: Box[\T\])` beside `tint[\T extends Blue\](x: Box[\T\])`, where `Red`, `Blue` and `Box` are objects. The checker refuses it, because `Box[\Bottom\]` lies in both domains, and walk loads it. No decision says which is right. Assert neither path's answer in a test (ledger row 786).
- A `where` clause's constraint: the checker checks a function's or functional method's constraint on its own static parameters at the call. At a dotted call, a candidate is not applicable where the receiver's static argument breaks the method's constraint. A trait's or object's own constraint is checked where its type is used, also at a constructor call; only the checker reads it, and the compiled code does not check it. A `where`-clause variable is a static parameter of the function's arrow type, inferred at the call. The checker does not yet check these, and no ledger row holds the first two:

  - at a type's use, a constraint whose bound names a `where`-clause variable;

So `import A.{...}` beside `import B.{ pick }`, where both apis declare `pick(x: P)`, is refused: 'There are multiple declarations of pick' (ledger row 813). The checker lets a member that it checked under the condition be called where the condition fails (ledger row 773).

## The `fortress` commands

`Shell.java` dispatches `bin/fortress <command>`.

- To see what an early phase makes of a program, stop after that phase: `parse` (a syntax check), `disambiguate`, `grammar`, `desugar` or `typecheck`.
- `unparse` prints the syntax tree back as Fortress source. Use it to see what a desugaring made.
- `link` links a compiled component (the `link` step of a compiled `.test` file). `api` writes a component's api. `test` runs a program's `test` declarations under walk.
- The command chooses the library. Walk and `test` call `Shell.useInterpreterLibraries()`. Every other command calls `useCompilerLibraries()`. Each call points `WellKnownNames` and `Types` to its prelude, and sets the desugaring switches.

## Running

    cd ProjectFortress
    # after an ant compileAll that started the caches again: the library order (build-and-caches.md)
    ../bin/fortress compile <path>/P.fss
    ../bin/fortress run P [args]

A small program compiles in about 5 s and runs in about 1 s.

- A crash of the checker prints one line and hides the Java stack. To see the stack, put `-debug stacktrace` before the file: `../bin/fortress compile -debug stacktrace <path>/P.fss`.
- A failed compile of a program leaves a 0-byte jar in `bytecode_cache/`. A run of the program then prints "Could not load P" and "Resource not found". Read the compile's error instead: it gives the cause.

## Before an edit

Two notes under `explorations/coordinator/map/` help you find where a fix belongs. Both date from September 2026, so a status or a line number in them can be stale. Before you rely on a status, read the ledger rows that it cites. Before you rely on a line number, grep for the method's name.

- Before you add or fix a language feature, print its row of the feature table. WORD names the feature, such as `spawn`, `coercion` or `typecase`. A row is about 1 KB. It names the feature's section of the specification, its parser rule, checker class, walk site, code-generator site, prelude declaration and ledger rows.

      explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'map:spec-to-implementation.md#Feature by feature@WORD'

- If your edit is in one phase, and you need what runs before and after it on each path, print that phase's section. Name the section by its number and the first word of its title. A section is 1 to 3 KB. B.1 is the phase list, B.4 disambiguation, B.5 desugaring, B.6 type checking, B.7 overloading, B.10 the caches, B.11 the runtime and B.12 the natives.

      explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'map:modules-and-phases.md#B.5 Desugaring'

- Before you change the text of a diagnostic, grep the `.test` files for it. A `.test` file can pin a whole diagnostic with `compile_err_equals`, its `file:line:column` included. `grep -l 'TEXT' ProjectFortress/*tests/*.test`, with words of the diagnostic as TEXT, lists the files that pin it. Update each of those in the same commit. A line that you add to or remove from a compiler test program moves the pinned spans below it.

## Testing an edit here

- For a quick loop on an edit of the checker or the code generator, compile the edited class into a scratch directory, and run the compiler with that directory first on its class path. This takes seconds, rebuilds nothing and changes nothing tracked. Give each run a fresh copy of the caches, because nothing checks the caches against the compiler that wrote them, and a compile of an unchanged program with a jar writes nothing:

      Q=$PWD/tmp/quick ; export FORTRESS_CACHES=$Q/caches ; CP=$(bin/fortress_classpath | tail -1)
      mkdir -p $Q/classes && javac -nowarn -cp "$CP" -d $Q/classes ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/<path>/X.java

      bin/fortress run P

- If your change is near transactions, top-level mutable state or the class loader's first load, do the four-thread atomic runs (`gate.md`).

## The checker's time

This section is for a change of the checker: its Scala under `scala_src/`, or `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast` and the generators under `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/astgen/`, from which the build generates the checker's syntax tree and `Walker`.

The count stage takes `<out-file> <scratch>` and about 80 to 180 seconds, more under load. It can run past the Bash tool's 120-second limit, so run it in the background (`session.md`). It writes a table to the out-file: the errors of each api, the total, the number of places with errors, and the first crash. It keeps the checker's whole output in `<scratch>/run.txt`, and its caches in `<scratch>`, so a run from the base build leaves the base build as it was.

The checker checks every api first, and the component only if no api has an error. In each api or component, it stops at the first of its stages that finds errors. The stages run in this order (`compiler/StaticChecker.java`, `checkCompilationUnit`):

1. The type hierarchy and the type check.
2. The overloading check, which also compares the overloads' return types.
3. In the component only, the export check (`library.md`, "Designing a change").

So the count misses the errors of the later stages, and a fix of an early error can raise it.

The table's rows tell a clean run from a run that the checker did not finish:

- `#total 0` and `#locations 0`: the checker reached the component and found no error.
- `#stopped`, in place of `#total` and `#locations`: the errors came from a phase before the checker, such as the parse. The checker reported none and did not reach the component. The script exits 1, and the gate reads the table as red.
- `#crash`: the first crash of the overloading check that the run survived, or `none`.

If the run printed no error total and was not clean, the script writes no table and exits 1.

The checker's results are the programs that it accepts and refuses, and each error with its text and its place. On the interpreter's library, a change keeps the results the same if both of these hold:

- The two tables are equal: `diff` prints nothing.

# The interpreter (walk)

Walk's code is in `interpreter/`:

- `evaluator/`: the tree walker.
- `env/`: the environments, which map names to values, and the wrappers that load components and apis.
- `rewrite/`: walk's own rewrite of the tree.
- `glue/`: the natives.

## How walk evaluates a program

After the phases (`SKILL.md`, "The phases"), walk rewrites each component in `interpreter/rewrite/`: it gives each reference to a name the lexical depth of its declaration. The evaluator looks up the name by that depth. The compiled path has no such rewrite.

At a call of a generic function, walk infers the static arguments from the run-time types of the arguments (`interpreter/evaluator/EvaluatorBase.java`, `inferAndInstantiateGenericFunction`). Each static parameter gets an interval, from a lower to an upper bound, in a `LatticeIntervalMap` (`useful/`). A type in the domain of an arrow type, such as `T` in `T -> ZZ32`, is contravariant. So its bounds go into the dual map, `LatticeIntervalMapDual`: the same table, with the order reversed. `MakeInferenceSpecific` then makes the inferences more specific, in practice only in the dual map.

Walk chooses a coercion by the value at run time. The specification and the compiled path choose it statically. Walk has no static types, so it cannot choose statically. The expected-failure tests `ProjectFortress/tests/XXXCoercionStaticRungC.fss` and `XXXCoercionStaticNarrowRungC.fss` record the difference.

Walk keeps a float numeral as a `FloatLiteral`, a type of its own, also where it is bound to an `RR64` variable, parameter or field. So `SEQV` finds it unequal to a computed `RR64` of the same bits. This `false` follows the rule that values of different types are never equivalent, and no ledger row holds it (F-326). For `value object V(f: RR64)` with no `=` of its own, `x: RR64 = 0.25 + 0.25` and `y: RR64 = 0.5`, `V(0.5) = V(x)` is `false`. So is `(y, 1, 2, 3) = (x, 1, 2, 3)`, since the library declares `=` on pairs and triples only. Give the value object its own `=` and make it extend `Equality[\V\]`, or compare the parts.

## Where a fix of walk belongs

Both paths run the same desugaring phases. Inside them, switches in `Shell.java` decide which desugarings run. Walk turns off these desugarings, which the compiled path runs:

- coercion;
- chained comparisons;
- compound and tuple assignment, and subscripts;
- case expressions, typecase and type ascription;
- the marking of a bodiless declaration as abstract.

Walk evaluates those nodes itself, in `interpreter/evaluator/Evaluator.java` (`forChainExpr`, `forAssignment`, `forCaseExpr`, `forTypecase`, `forAsExpr`). It converts by coercion at dispatch, in `OverloadedFunction.bestMatchWithCoercion`. So if walk is wrong on one of these nodes, fix the evaluator, not the desugarer.

An edit of a phase that both paths run, or of the desugaring switches, can change both paths. An edit under `interpreter/` changes walk only.

## What walk checks

Walk does not check static types (`SKILL.md`, "The phases"). The commands that stop after a phase, and `unparse`, use the compiler's prelude and the compiled path's desugaring switches (`compiler.md`, "The `fortress` commands"). So `fortress typecheck` does not check a walk program, and `desugar` or `unparse` does not print the tree that walk runs. That tree is the component's entry in `interpreter_cache/` (`SKILL.md`, "The caches").

Under walk, the disambiguator, the phase that binds names, refuses a program's own top-level type that has the name of a type of `FortressLibrary`, such as `Index` or `Indexed`: "Type name may refer to: Index, FortressLibrary.Index". Give such a type another name.

At load, walk checks the overload sets, some `comprises` clauses, inherited abstract methods and `override` declarations. It lifts each object expression to the top level as an object, which takes the static parameters of an enclosing generic function, and checks it as an object. It checks a trait or object with static parameters once, through a stand-in: one type for all its instances, with a symbolic type for each static parameter (`symbolicInstance` in `interpreter/evaluator/BuildEnvironments.java`). Through the stand-in, it does not check two functional methods whose parameter types mention a symbolic type. It makes no stand-in, and so checks nothing through one, for a declaration with an `opr` static parameter, or where its static parameters, `where` clause or `extends` clause raise an error at the symbolic types. It refuses:

- two declarations of one name that its parameter-by-parameter check cannot order. It accepts them if `comprises` clauses cover the overlap. For every pair of functions of which at least one is generic, it checks the overloading rules of `SKILL.md`, "Fortress as a language", on their declared domains (`revival-changes.md`, "Dispatch and overloading"): the No Duplicates Rule, the Meet Rule and the Return Type Rule. So it refuses two whose declared domains are equal. The message names the rule: "fails because their parameter lists have the same types", "fails the Return Type Rule" or "fails the Meet Rule". Walk keeps the team's check and messages for the pairs below. The team's check looks for a position where the two parameter types neither nest nor exclude. If a parameter type there mentions a static parameter, the message is "at least one pair of parameters must have excluding types". If neither does, it is "are unrelated (neither subtype, excludes, nor equal) and no excluding pair is present". The pairs:
  - a pair with a varargs parameter;
  - a pair whose parameter lists differ in length, only where one of them has a varargs parameter. Walk checks no other pair of lists of different lengths;
  - a pair that is neither two generic declarations, nor a generic one beside a plain one, nor a generic function beside a generic trait's or object's functional method that has no static parameters of its own;
  - the instances of an explicit instantiation.

  Where it reads exclusion over the whole tuple of parameter types, at the instance that the equalities force, it reads two parameter types that still mention a static parameter as excluding only where no instances of the two can meet. Walk departs from the rules in these cases:
  - At load, it does not check two functional methods of a generic trait or object on their declared domains. It compares them at each call, on the instance that the call makes. So such a pair that breaks the rules loads, and a call can fail with "Cannot find definition for method" (ledger row 780).
  - It refuses two generic functional methods whose declared domains lie one inside the other, in a type without static parameters (ledger row 779).
  - It refuses a pair whose overlap it finds only through an instance of a supertype, also where a third declaration covers the overlap (ledger row 539).
  - It refuses overloads on two instantiations of one generic type, as `g(b: Tg[\3\])` beside `g(b: Tg[\4\])` (ledger row 416).
  - Its parameter-by-parameter check reads an object type over a static parameter as excluding a type that one of its instances is or extends. So it loads `g[\T\](x: Box[\T\], y: ZZ32)` beside `g(x: Box[\ZZ32\], y: Any)`, which the Meet Rule refuses (ledger row 788).
  - It reads no `where` clause when it reads exclusion over the whole tuple. So it refuses such a pair where one declaration has a `where` clause of its own (ledger row 787).
  - It does not refuse a type that extends a self-typed trait `T[\A\]` and is not an `A` (`revival-changes.md`, "Traits and objects"). A call that both `T`'s operator and another declaration fit then runs one of them, without an ambiguity error (ledger row 893). Make each type that extends `T[\A\]` an `A`.
  - It loads a generic top-level function whose declared domain lies inside that of a self-typed trait's functional method of the same name, where the Return Type Rule holds. The checker refuses every top-level function more specific than a functional method of its name, a check that the specification does not state: '… is more specific than the declaration of the functional method' (ledger row 894).
  - It loads a function over `Index` beside one over a pair whose element types neither lie below `Index` nor exclude it, which the Meet Rule refuses (ledger row 806).
  - It loads a type that provides two functional symbolic operators, such as two `||`, that break the Meet Rule for Functional Methods (`Specification/advanced/overloading.tex`). The checker refuses the pair (ledger row 611).

  The paths differ on `f[\T extends { K, R[\T\] }\](x: T)` beside `f(x: Z)`, where `K comprises { A, B, C }`, `Z excludes { A, B }`, and `C` is an object that extends `Z` but not `R`. Walk refuses the pair: "fails the Meet Rule". The checker reads the bounds, finds that no value lies in both domains, and accepts it. No decision says which is right. Assert neither path's answer in a test (ledger row 713).
- two functional methods that break the Meet Rule for Functional Methods in a type that provides both, where their name is an identifier or an operator named by a word, as `MAX`.
- an overloaded function with one parameter of type `T`, where `T extends Any` is written: `f[\T extends Any\](x: T)`.
- an extender that a `comprises` clause of the program's main component does not allow. Walk does not yet check the library's clauses, another component's clauses or an object expression's clauses. Where a listed type names a bounded type `where`-clause variable, as `NBox[\E\]` in `comprises { NBox[\E\] } where [\E extends Number\]`, walk ignores the variable's bound, and runs `NBox[\String\]` (ledger row 754). In another declaration's bound, it takes a name equal to the variable's as the variable (ledger row 778).
- a trait whose `comprises` clause lists a type at a `where`-clause variable, where a member's declared type names the variable: "Missing type E" (ledger row 755).
- an object or object expression without static parameters that inherits an abstract method and does not define it. Bodies define it if they are at or below its parameter types and together cover them, with `comprises` clauses read. Walk also refuses where its search for a cover does not settle: at a cycle of `comprises` clauses, at a symbolic type, or beyond 10,000 steps or 4,096 combinations of listed types. It also refuses a valid object whose one body for the method has a static parameter of its own (ledger row 728).
- a declaration with the modifier `override`, in a trait, object or object expression, that overrides no declaration that its type's immediate supertraits provide. An `override` at an inherited declaration's own parameter types overrides nothing. At an instance of a generic trait above a declared object, equal parameter types count as overridden. Walk does not read all the bounds of the static parameters in two cases:
  - an object expression, which takes its static parameters from the function around it;
  - a generic trait or object that extends a type under a `where` clause.

  In these cases, walk does not refuse an `override` if the inherited declaration's parameter types mention a static parameter and differ from the `override`'s.

So a library edit can stop every program at load, if it does one of these:

- adds an overload;
- leaves an inherited abstract method that no bodies cover, covers it only by a body with a static parameter of its own, or covers it by bodies whose cover walk's search cannot settle;
- adds an `override` that overrides nothing;
- gives a member a type that names its trait's `comprises`-clause variable, as `E` in `AnyList`;
- names, in a `builtinPrimitive` string, a helper that walk refuses ("Natives").

Walk checks a program's declarations against the library's only when it analyses the library, not when it loads the library's entries from the cache (ledger row 342). So a program that walk refuses with an empty cache runs with a filled one. Deleting the program's own entries does not bring the check back. To see such a refusal, run with an empty cache, as `COLD_CACHE=1` gives `harness-one.sh`.

Walk compares no component with the apis that it exports. So a component that leaves out an api member, or declares it at another header, loads and runs under walk. The compiled export check refuses it (ledger row 841). `library.md`, "Designing a change", gives the step that runs the check on each component.

`tests-writing.md` says how a test names a refusal at load.

Walk's overload-ambiguity message names its two declarations in an order that varies from run to run. On one core, the order is fixed for a given library, but a library edit can change it. Do not pin or compare this order. The harness reads only that an `XXX` test fails.

## Natives

The library binds each of walk's natives by a declaration whose body is `builtinPrimitive("…")`. The string names one of these:

- A glue class, as `com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.X`, in `interpreter/glue/prim/`. A glue class takes walk's `FValue` objects, so the compiled path cannot use it.
- A helper: a public static method of a class under `nativeHelpers/`, as `com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleIntArith.<method>`. `interpreter/glue/StaticNativeApp.java` calls it by reflection, with a method's `self` first. The compiled path calls it too (`compiler.md`, "Natives"). Most bindings name a helper. The others name a glue class. F-299 counts both kinds (`records.md`, "Reading the record").

Walk carries each declared type of a helper's binding in one Java type:

- `ZZ32`, `NN32` and `Char` in `int`; `ZZ64` and `NN64` in `long`; `RR64` and `Float`, the library's object that extends `RR64`, in `double`; `RR32` in `float`; `Boolean` in `boolean`;
- `FlatString` and `JavaString` in `String`, and `String` too, except as a parameter other than `self`; `ZZ` in `BigInteger`; `()` in `void`; `JavaBufferedWriter`, the library's writer trait, in `compiler/runtimeValues/FortressBufferedWriter`, which the checker reads back as `JavaBufferedWriter`.

In a method, walk carries `self` by the type that declares the method:

- a type of the list above, except `JavaString` and `()`, in the same Java type, but `FlatString` only where it is the library's own;
- the library's objects that extend number types, not the glue classes of the same names: `Int` (`ZZ32`) in `int`, `Long` (`ZZ64`) and `UnsignedLong` (`NN64`) in `long`, and `BigNum` (`ZZ`) in `BigInteger`.

A program can give its own type the name `FlatString` or `JavaString`. Walk tells the library's `FlatString` by the component that declares it, so a program's own type of either name carries no `self`. But walk carries a parameter declared at such a type in `String`, by the type's name alone, and does not refuse the binding. The native then receives the name of the type, not the value's text (ledger row 877). Give a program's own type another name.

Walk refuses a helper's binding at load in these cases. The message names the string, and contains the words below, which a `load_exception_contains` key can match:

- The class or the method does not exist: 'not found' or 'names no static method of'.
- The result type, or a parameter type other than `self`'s, is not carried by the first list: 'no Java type carries the declared'.
- The binding is in a method of a type that the second list does not name, as a program's own object: 'no Java type carries T, the type of self.', with the type's name as T. Match ', the type of self.' to tell it from the refusal above.
- No method of that name, or more than one, has exactly the Java types of the lists, with `self`'s first in a method: 'has no overload that fits the declaration's types', or 'overloads that fit'.

The check has two gaps:

- Walk checks the binding of a dotted method of a generic trait or object only when the program makes an instance, at run time. So a program that makes no instance loads. One that makes an instance stops there with the same message, as an `InterpreterBug` (ledger row 864). Test such a binding with a program that makes an instance.
- Walk reads the type that declares the method, not the type of the value. So a program's object that extends `ZZ32` loads. A call of a method of `ZZ32` that binds a helper then stops with 'getInt not implemented for FOrdinaryObject' (ledger row 551).

A glue class bound over `String`, and a helper bound in a method of `String` as `self`, receive the wrong text for a `CatString`: the name of the type, not its characters (ledger row 846). `||` builds a `CatString` when the joined string is longer than `maxLeafSize`, 32 characters by default. Bind such a native over `FlatString`, and beside it an overload over `String` that passes `s.asFlatString`, as `printlnWithThread` does (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:4640-4644`). In a method of `String`, call that overload with `self`.

An `import java` written in a `.fss` file is wired under walk but unfinished, and no test uses it. The compiled path's generated `import java` (`compiler.md`, "Natives") is not this one.

A glue class raises a Fortress exception that a `catch` sees by throwing a `FortressError` that holds the exception's object. `Int.overflow()` in `interpreter/glue/prim/Int.java` makes one, and its callers throw it:

    FObject f = (FObject) Driver.getFortressLibrary().getRootValue(WellKnownNames.integerOverflowException);
    return new FortressError(f);

A helper runs on both paths, so it raises an exception as compiled code does: `throw Utility.makeFortressException("fortress.CompilerBuiltin$DivisionByZero")` (`compiler/runtimeValues/Utility.java`). The string names the compiler's prelude's class for the exception. Under walk, that class does not load, and `StaticNativeApp` raises the interpreter's library's object of the same name in its place. So raise from a helper only an exception that both libraries declare as an object, as `DivisionByZero` and `IntegerOverflow`. `DIV`, `REM` and `MOD` by zero on `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `NN32` and `NN64` raise `DivisionByZero` in this way, on both paths. So no division, remainder or modulus by zero on these types ends the run. A `catch` sees no other Java exception, so any other Java exception of a native, a glue class's included, ends the run.

## Running a program

    bin/fortress P.fss

- If the run stops on an error, it prints the error and the Fortress stack under `Context:`. The hint below them names `-debug interpreter`, which shows nothing more. To see the Java stack too, run `bin/fortress -debug stacktrace P.fss`.
- Walk searches for imports in the current directory first (`build-and-caches.md`, "Name resolution").
- If `JAVA_FLAGS` is not set, `bin/fortress` uses `-Xmx256m -Xss32m`. Your setup gives a 4 GB heap, and the test harness uses 768 MB. A test can pass at two of these heaps and die at the third. If you claim that a run fails near a memory limit, measure the claim at 256 MB: run with `JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx256m -Xss32m -Djava.io.tmpdir=$PWD/tmp"`.
- Your setup sets `FORTRESS_THREADS`, the size of the pool, to 1 (`SKILL.md`, "Parallelism and mutable state"). If it is unset, the pool has half the CPUs.
- A small program takes about 8 s with cold caches, and about 4 s with warm caches.
- Do not take or record a timing of walk. Do not edit anything to make walk faster.
- To check a build, run `bin/fortress explorations/claude_demo.fss`. It prints `SUM[i <- 1#100] i = 5050` among its lines, and exits 0. `ProjectFortress/hello.fss` runs only on the compiled path.

## The model program

MicroGPT runs only under walk, by hand, never in the gate. Check the model when your brief asks for it: run your tree's `explorations/coordinator/tools/mg-run.sh <work-dir> <label> [threads]`. `<work-dir>` is a folder under your tree's `tmp/`, and `threads` sets `FORTRESS_THREADS`, 1 by default. The script runs the quick pair at once, `MicroGptFlatQuick.fss` and `MicroGptAplQuick.fss`: two forward and backward passes each, against the reference values, in about 56 s for both. Each starts from an empty private cache and writes `<work-dir>/<name>.txt`. Read its `VERDICT:` line and its last line, `rc=`.

- Add the word `full` only if your brief asks for it. It runs the full pair, `MicroGptFlatCheck.fss` and `MicroGptAplCheck.fss`, with 40 checks each and a 90-minute timeout.
- If you change a line of the model, put the change in your report as a diff.

# The orientation workflow

The `fortress-repo` skill's revival part, `references/revival-changes.md`, becomes the **orientation**: the short account of how revived Fortress departs from the original and from what a model expects, which every worker reads whole (Astra's review, `explorations/reviews/revival-record-synthesis.md`). `orientation.js` writes it, in two modes:

- **consolidate**, once, and again whenever the part has drifted: an outline by the concepts workers use and a table of where each old entry goes (`outline.md`); the writer writes the whole text from them; a preservation check against the table, a cold read with only the skill's core, and the regression quiz; the writer's fix round; a second cold read and the quiz again; a judge.
- **update**, after every landing: the landing's new and changed FACTS and POSITIONS entries pass the admission test (`admission.md`: the wrong default, the correction, the mistake it prevents); the writer rewrites the sections they touch in place, within the budget of 8K to 12K characters; the same checks, fix round, reread and judge.

The writer is a headless Opus stream (`../record-clarity/writer-stream.sh`), so its fix round resumes the session that wrote the text. The regression quiz is kept in `regression/` (questions and key), and grows with each update.

## Running it

    Workflow({ scriptPath: '/home/user/fortress/explorations/coordinator/tools/orientation/orientation.js',
               args: { mode: 'consolidate', out: '/abs/folder/', stream: 'orientation', concepts: ['/abs/concepts.md'] } })
    Workflow({ scriptPath: ..., args: { mode: 'update', out: '/abs/folder/', stream: 'orientation-bN', facts: ['F-261', 'P-153'] } })

## Installing its result

The judge writes `judgement.md` and `queue.md`. The coordinator then has the skill writer (`skill-writer.sh`) install the sections judged "install" into `references/revival-changes.md`, add `sources-mapping.md` to the skill's `references/sources.md`, and, after a consolidation, update the core's line for the part and its description together; then a cold read of the installed part, as `coordinator/references/skill-rewrite.md` says. Held sections keep the old text; their items go to `review-queue.md`.
